Hey, I posted the PMs. I'm really sorry that some people feel that it's spam, and that the survey was unethical. Let me address the first, and then the second.

First, I think it's worth keeping in mind that spam is in the eye of the beholder. I got a couple enthusiastic responses from Voat users, saying "cool study, can't wait to see the results". I'd give the exact count, but all the PMs seemed to have disappeared. @Atko, you got "a few PMs from Voat users who got this spam PM" -- emphasis on "few". But, even if many people found the survey OK, I'm still sensitive to those users who felt that the PM constituted spam. I'm just trying to put it in perspective.

More concerning is that some people find the study "unethical". One of the difficult aspects of sociological research is that one cannot avoid affecting the social system one wishes to measure. Scientific research has externalities. Ethics is a discipline with rigourous methods. Science has come a long way in that respect. All studies involving human participants are subjected to a rigorous ethics review. In each case, it is a matter of balancing potential risks against gains. Our study is no different. A thorough ethics review was performed and it was found that the risks were minimal, and outweighed by the potential gains.

We were hoping is that Voat users might be interested in what the study finds -- based on the responses I got, I think that is actually how most Voat users felt.

But from a sociological perspective, what has happened recently with reddit, voat, and other sites like them, is truly fascinating. We think that there is an interesting story about how communities of discussion undergo change, crisis, birth, and bear the weight of a heavy September. This is a unique opportunity. I submit for you to consider whether being able to include this story among the pages of science was worth it.

Let me also explain why we sent out the PMs. In case you don't know, we also posted to AskVoat, where we got a positive response. However, posting in a public forum is likely to lead to self-selection bias, and the users who see the thread do not constitute a random sample. So, we drew a random sample of 500 users to whom we sent the message.

@Atko, to be completely frank, I highly doubt you would have responded to us if we said "Hey, we want to survey users of voat, can you help us". But I don't know you; I could be wrong. I guess I'll never know.

Additionally, informed consent requires a great many things, not least of which is an understanding of precisely what data will be gathered, what the intended purpose of the survey or experiment is, whether it is confidential or anonymous or even semi-public, and almost invariably followed by a de-briefing in the more serious surveys/experiments.

To do as this person has done, without total disclosure of these considerations a priori, is to denigrate the criterion for informed consent, and it is severely in breach of convention and expectation of sociological procedure and also ethics.

Human beings are not lab rats. There are bare minimum standards, no matter whose delicate sensibilities - or brash disregard for others - is offended by those standards.

(And yes, some phone surveys - if they do not garner truly informed consent, or otherwise skew their methodology - are unethical.)
